newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton says NATO-bound Poland is "coming home".
newsitem.headline: Clinton says NATO-bound Poland is "coming home".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton congratulated Poland on Thursday on its prospective entry into NATO, saying that eight years after the collapse of communism in Central Europe's largest state: "Poland is coming home."

Addressing a flag-waving crowd of thousands in a part of Warsaw rebuilt from the rubble of World War Two, Clinton said the country of 38 million had earned the right to be an ally of the Western democracies "and to the destiny you deserve".

"Now Poland is joining NATO," he said. "Poland is taking its place in the community of democracy. Never again will your fate be decided by others. Never again will the birthright of freedom be denied you. Poland is coming home!" he said.
It was in Poland that Solidarity in 1980 won recognition as the Soviet bloc's first free trade union, giving teetering Soviet power a push that helped bring its collapse in 1989.

Clinton came to this capital straight from Madrid, where he and other NATO leaders earlier this week agreed to invite Poland, Hungary and the the Czech Republic to join the world's most powerful security pact. They said the alliance would be open to others, including Romania and Slovenia.
"Other nations are counting on you to show the contributions new members can make," Clinton told Poles gathered on the city's Castle Square.
"You did not walk through NATO's door to see it shut behind you. That door will stay open," he added.

Among those accompanying the U.S. president to Warsaw was Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who was born in the Czech Republic, and Senator Barbara Mikulski, a Maryland Democrat whose grandparents came from Poland.
Clinton, who held talks with Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski before the speech, coupled congratulatory rhetoric with sober words about the responsibilities of NATO membership.
"The struggle for democracy is never over. It must be fought every day," he said.

Kwasniewski, a former Communist official, anticipated the warning in his speech. "The invitation to NATO is an accomplishment, but at the same time it is a challenge," he said. "We are all aware of the tasks ahead of us and the cost. Security does not come free."
Poland's tasks include making its 230,000-strong armed forces compatible with NATO's air control, command and communications standards -- costing $3 billion over 15 years.

Poland must spend much more modernising and re-equipping its forces, and is now working out how much it can afford. It hopes for financial support from its allies and good terms for its industry if it opts for major arms purchases like the 100 new fighter aircraft its military wants.

Before yielding the podium to Clinton, Kwasniewski saluted several Polish fighters for democracy including Solidarity founder Lech Walesa, who, in a cruel trick of fate, found himself sitting in the audience while his ex-communist adversary got the limelight.
Walesa, a former Polish president and early proponent of NATO membership for his country, got a resounding ovation when his successor paid tribute to him.
He later met Clinton and told reporters he had thanked the U.S. leader but told him: "We have to finish this task, this is just the beginning."
The Warsaw celebrations were overshadowed by floods in southern Poland which have killed more than 20 people and taken priority even over the NATO developments in Polish news media.

The acclamation of Poland's entry into NATO included lavish praise for the United States from several speakers, including a young Polish officer who studied at the U.S. Air Force Academy and an elderly Polish veteran of World War Two who fought against the Germans commanding an American-built tank.

"We share two hundred years of military tradition of fighting for freedom," veteran Boleslaw Kukielka told Clinton, citing Polish soldiers who supported the American revolution like General Thadeusz Kosciuszko.
"Thanks, Bill," said a sign in the crowd, hailing Clinton's role in the move to embark on NATO's biggest expansion in its 48-years history.
Not all the signs were friendly, however. "Clinton, Murderer of the Unborn," said another, referring to Clinton's support for the right of women to obtain an abortion.
